tasks.currentSketch: Build squares on the sides of the right triangle. The altitude-parallel through the right-angle vertex cuts each half of the hypotenuse square into a triangle equal in area to one leg square's corresponding triangle; base and height show each constructed parallelogram is twice its triangle. Adding the two equalities gives c²=a²+b².

tasks.entryDescription: Euclid's product-plus-one; Euler's harmonic-series/Euler-product argument; Furstenberg's topology on the integers; analytic counting arguments. A historical survey catalogs about 200 variants.
tasks.currentSketch: Let S=Z with the topology generated by all two-sided arithmetic progressions. Each progression is clopen, so any finite union of progressions is closed. Let A be the union of pZ over all primes p. Every integer except −1 and 1 is divisible by a prime, hence Z\A={−1,1}; this two-point set is not open in this topology, so A is not closed. Thus A cannot be a finite union of the closed sets pZ, and there must be infinitely many primes.

tasks.currentSketch: For s>1, unique factorization gives ζ(s)=∏ₚ(1−p^(−s))⁻¹. If there were finitely many primes, the right side would remain bounded as s↓1, whereas ζ(s)=Σn⁻ˢ diverges by comparison with ∫₁∞x⁻ˢdx. Contradiction. This is an analytic Euler-product proof and overlaps route 3-r2; it is not a distinct strategy unless the ζ-function argument is developed separately.

tasks.currentSketch: For a fixed modulus m, let P be the finite set of primes dividing m or a₁⋯aₖ. Choose N divisible by m and by all listed primes, and consider aN+1; any prime divisor q is new and q∤aN. This alone controls only q∤m when q is chosen with additional congruence constraints; a general product-plus-one is insufficient to force q≡a (mod m). The route is valid only for specially engineered progressions, as the catalog says.

tasks.currentSketch: For a suitable cyclotomic value Φ_n(A), any prime divisor not dividing nA has multiplicative order n modulo q, hence n|(q−1), so q≡1 (mod n). Taking A arbitrarily large yields new such prime divisors; exclude finitely many exceptional divisors by choosing A. This establishes infinitely many primes ≡1 mod n, not arbitrary reduced residue classes.
